## Synopsis: Definition of Microsurgery
- Microsurgery and supermicrosurgery refer to the surgical coaptation of small vessels.
- Usually around 1 mm in diameter or smaller, under microscope magnification.
- A broad term not limited to blood vessels.
- Also refers to coaptation of tiny nerves and lymphatics.

## Synopsis: Evolution of Microsurgery
- Evolved significantly over the last four decades.
- Started from revascularization and replantation in 1960.
- Progressed to free flap surgery.

## Synopsis: Key Developments
- Development of the operating microscope.
- Advancements in microinstruments.
- Creation of ultra-fine sutures.
- These greatly aided its widespread use.

## Synopsis: Common Techniques
- Most commonly used techniques:
  - End-to-end anastomosis
  - End-to-side anastomosis
  - Coupling devices
- Difficult situations can usually be overcome with special techniques.

## Synopsis: Difficult Situations
- Vessel diameter discrepancy
- Inadequate vessel length
- Poor vessel quality

## Synopsis: Success & Cost-Effectiveness
- Advances lead to consistently high success rates.
- Made free tissue transfer a cost-effective, first-line option.
- Superior results and high patient satisfaction compared to conventional methods.

## Synopsis: Demands of Microsurgery
- Mentally and physically demanding.
- The need for special training cannot be overemphasized.
- Thorough preoperative planning is mandatory.
- Flexibility of the surgical plan and flawless execution are required.

## Synopsis: Monitoring & Pharmacological Agents
- Clinical assessment remains the gold standard in free flap monitoring.
- Early detection of a failing free flap with prompt intervention improves salvage rates.
- Pharmacological agents: low-dose heparin, PGE1, and dextran are useful.

## Synopsis: Complications & Success Rates
- Complications are not only due to vascular compromise.
- Inadequate planning, inappropriate flap selection, and flawed execution can compromise outcomes.
- Refined techniques and specialized ICUs lead to 96–98% success rates in developed centers.

## Synopsis: Future Directions
- Microsurgery will not decline but continue to evolve.
- Revolutionized our approach to reconstructive challenges.
- Wider application in:
  - Supermicrosurgery
  - Free-style free flaps
  - Composite tissue allotransplantation

## Introduction: Definition & Scope
- General term for surgery requiring the operating microscope or high magnification loupes.
- Terms coined depending on structure:
  - Microvascular surgery (blood vessels around 1 mm)
  - Microneural surgery
  - Microlymphatic surgery
  - Microtubular surgery

## Introduction: Supramicrosurgery
- An extreme form of microsurgery.
- Refers to anastomoses of vessels around 0.5 mm in diameter (0.3–0.8 mm).
- Common in:
  - Lymphatic reconstruction
  - Perforator-to-perforator anastomosis/perforator repair
  - Distal digital replantation

## Introduction: Reconstructive Microsurgery
- Utilizes microsurgical and supramicrosurgical techniques.
- Procedures: revascularization, replantation, auto- or allotransplantation.
- Solves problems from traumatic injuries, congenital deformities, and tumor ablation.

## Introduction: Magnification Options
- Some procedures performed under loupe magnification (×2.5–8).
- Includes vessels and nerves coaptation.
- Especially when diameter is not too small (usually around 2–3 mm).

## Introduction: Scope in Plastic Surgery
- Techniques not limited to plastic surgery.
- However, the scope of practice within plastic surgery remains the most diverse in modern surgery.

## Introduction: Historical Beginnings
- Era began with the invention of the microscope in 1920.
- Improvement in magnification and illumination.
- Development of microinstruments and ultrafine sutures.
- Leading factors for widespread use.

## Introduction: Changing Approaches
- Consistently reported high success rates of 97–100%.
- Cost-effectiveness and superior outcomes.
- Changed indication from last resort to first choice.
- Reversed and overthrew the reconstructive ladder in advanced centers.

## Introduction: Current Demands
- Success and widespread application demands experience and resources.
- Professional training, specialized infrastructures, dedication, and support ensure high-volume microsurgery.

## Historical Perspective: Early Concepts
- Concept of vascular repair first proposed by Paré in 1552.
- First successful brachial artery repair performed in 1759.
- 1897: Murphy reported successful end-to-end anastomosis of femoral artery by invagination with fine silk.

## Historical Perspective: Alexis Carrel
- 1902: Alexis Carrel reported technical breakthrough for end-to-end vascular anastomoses using triangulation method.
- Expanded in collaboration with Guthrie.
- Awarded Nobel Prize in 1912 for "vascular suture and transplantation of blood vessels and organs".

## Historical Perspective: Giant Leaps Forward
- Experimental limb replantation in dogs and models.
- Isolation of heparin from the liver by McLean.
- Clinical introduction of heparin as an anticoagulant.
- Use of the operating microscope gave microvascular surgery a giant leap forward.

## Historical Perspective: The Microscope
- Compound microscope invented by Janssen in 1590.
- Mass-produced by Carl Zeiss for lab research in late 1800s.
- 1921: Carl-Olof Siggesson Nylen first used modified monocular Brinell–Leitz microscope for animal surgery.

## Historical Perspective: Binocular Microscopes
- Nylen’s microscope soon replaced by binocular microscope.
- Developed in 1922 by colleague Gunnar Holmgren.
- 1946: Perritt applied use of microscope to ophthalmology.

## Historical Perspective: Modern Microvascular Surgery
- 1960: Vascular surgeons Jacobson and Suarez introduced the diploscope.
- Stereoscopic microscope for simultaneous use by two surgeons.
- Anastomoses of vessels as small as 1 mm in diameter.
- Extensive use in peripheral nerve, plastic, experimental transplantation, and neurosurgery.

## Historical Perspective: First Clinical Replantations
- First clinical application was in replantation.
- 1964: Malt and McKhann reported successful replantation of several arms.
- 1965: Konatsu and Tamai performed first complete thumb replantation with microscope aid.

## Historical Perspective: Toe-to-Hand Transfers
- 1966: Young reported series of second toe-to-hand transfers.
- 1967: Cobbett performed first successful great toe-to-thumb transfer in a human being.

## Historical Perspective: First Free Flaps
- 1965: Krizek et al. transplanted experimental flaps based on superficial epigastric vessels in dogs.
- 1971: Antia performed first clinical free flap (dermolipomatous groin flap), complicated by infection.
- 1970: McLean and Buncke reported first fully successful free flap (omental free flap).
- 1973: Daniel and Taylor reported transfer of first groin flap.

## Historical Perspective: Perforator & Free-Style Flaps
- Late 1980s: Cutaneous flaps based on perforator vessels evolved from conventional musculocutaneous flaps.
- 1989: Koshima and Soeda reported first true perforator flap (deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap).
- Next milestone: Free-style flap based on audible perforator detected by hand-held Doppler.

## Historical Perspective: Allotransplantation
- 1998: First successful hand transplantation in Lyon, France.
- 1999: First in Louisville, USA.
- 2005: First partial face transplantation in Lyon, France.
- 2010: First total face transplantation in Barcelona, Spain.
- Widespread application depends more on immunosuppression than microsurgery advances.

## Tools: Magnification & Illumination
- Accurate perception of operative anatomy.
- Improved outcomes and facilitation of impossible procedures.
- Reduces surgeons’ fatigue due to improved ergonomics.
- Two types of optical systems: surgical microscope and loupes.

## Tools: Surgical Microscopes - Basic Features
- Binocular head with adjustable eyepieces.
- Teaching head allows two people to work with magnification.
- Third head possible for digital recording.
- Heads independently pivot with separate magnification levels.

## Tools: Surgical Microscopes - Controls
- Tilt, focus, and zoom controlled via foot pedal or hand control panel.
- Foot pedal keeps hands free but necessitates coordination.
- Hand control panel keeps all functions in one accessible place.
- Antimicrobial-coated surfaces and internally routed cables are important.

## Tools: Surgical Microscopes - Magnification
- Up to 62× magnifications with instant magnification change.
- Variable working distance (e.g., 10× eyepiece and 200 mm objective lens).
- Final magnification range from 4.4 to 50.4.
- Some incorporate intraoperative fluorescence tools (e.g., Leica, OPMI Pentero).

## Tools: Surgical Microscopes - Mounting
- Mounted on a stand, placed on table top, or worn on surgeon’s head.
- Hung on ceiling or wall to conserve floor space.
- Mobile microscopes desired for cost-effectiveness across specialties.

## Tools: Choosing Magnification
- Low magnification (6×–12×): Vessel preparation and suture tying.
- Middle magnification (15×–19×): Suture placement.
- High magnification: Very small vessel anastomosis and inspection.

## Tools: Box 25.1 Tips for Microscopes (Part 1)
- Familiarize yourself with the microscope.
- Spend time getting position right (interpupillary distance, diopter correction).
- Use adjustable seat if sitting.
- Sit comfortably with feet flat on ground for stable base.

## Tools: Box 25.1 Tips for Microscopes (Part 2)
- Upper extremities well supported, resting on folded drapes.
- Minimizes fatigue and tremor.
- Focus adjusted with scope at highest magnification before starting.

## Tools: Loupes - Overview
- Magnifications of 2.5×–8×.
- Mounted on glasses or headbands.
- Cost-effective, portable, offer operator freedom.
- Invaluable for precise dissection and placement of instruments.

## Tools: Loupes vs. Microscope Study
- Retrospective study of 200 consecutive free microvascular tissue transplantations.
- Compared 3.5× loupes and operating microscope.
- No difference in outcome: 99% success rate for both groups.
- Microscopes required for children and vessels ≤1.5 mm.

## Tools: Types of Loupes - Compound
- Compound (Galilean) loupe.
- Two magnifying lenses separated by air.
- Higher magnification, greater depth of field, better working distance.
- Image distortion above 2.5× and "halo" effect at periphery.
- Low cost and light weight.

## Tools: Types of Loupes - Prismatic
- Prismatic loupe uses Schmidt prism.
- Lengthens path of light through mirror reflections.
- Improved magnification, wider fields of view, longer depths of field.
- 30–40% heavier, more expensive, easily damaged.

## Tools: Choosing Loupes - Magnification
- 2.5× sufficient for hand surgery and flap harvesting.
- 3.5–4.5× suitable for perforator dissection, thin flaps, or anastomoses.
- Field of view and depth of field decrease with increasing magnification.
- Weight increases; >4.5× tends to be cumbersome and cause neck tension.

## Tools: Choosing Loupes - Features
- Lens design, working angle, and distances.
- Mounted on glasses or headbands.
- Through-the-lens vs. flip-up or snap-fit type.
- Flip-up permits cheaper changing of magnification and lens prescription.
- Headlights available for additional lighting.

## Tools: Microsurgical Instruments - Essential Features
- Fine tips to spread, hold, or cut delicate tissue and suture.
- Nonreflective surface.
- Comfortable handles that close easily to prevent fatigue.
- Spring-loaded; choosing right spring tension is important.

## Tools: Microsurgical Instruments - Materials
- Heat-hardened stainless steel (resistant to wear and tear).
- Prone to magnetization; store on demagnetized shelves.
- Demagnetizer coil used if magnetized.
- Antimagnetic materials like titanium becoming popular (rust-free, lighter).

## Tools: Microsurgical Instruments - Handles & Length
- Round or flat handle.
- Range from 10–18 cm in length.
- Shorter instruments for surface anastomosis (e.g., hand surgery).
- Longer instruments (>18 cm) for free tissue transfer.
- Longer instruments may be balanced to reduce fatigue.

## Tools: Microsurgical Instruments - Maintenance
- Follow manufacturer instructions.
- Store in specially designed cases.
- Protect fine tips with silicone or rubber tubes.
- Clean blood/contaminants regularly; rinse with distilled/deionized water.
- Avoid high chloride concentrations to prevent pitting and corrosion.

## Tools: Scissors
- Spring-loaded with sharp but gently curved blades.
- Slightly rounded tips.
- Held closed, used safely as dissecting probe.
- Straight blades with sharp tips for trimming adventitia and stitch-cutting.
- One curve scissor is usually adequate for both tasks.

## Tools: Needle Holders
- Spring-loaded, held like pencils, resting on first web.
- Handle ideally rounded to roll needle between fingers.
- Jaws thin and gently curved with narrow shoulders.
- Curved style finer at tip, suitable for vessel dilatation.

## Tools: Needle Holders - Ratchets & Supermicrosurgery
- Ratchet lock facilitates parking and passing needle.
- Inexperienced hands may damage needle with ratchets; unlocking preferred.
- Supermicrosurgery: Titanium preferred for lighter weight.
- Allows order-specific manufacturing for flexible, tight grip without needle bending.

## Tools: Forceps - Jeweler's Forceps
- Originally designed by Swiss Dumont factory.
- Flat handle and sharply narrowing tips.
- Tips aligned with precision of 1/1000 inch.
- Jaws meet evenly over 3 mm length under moderate pressure.

## Tools: Forceps - Types & Uses
- Classified by width of contact surface, narrowness, configuration.
- Wide jaws can be used as needle holders.
- Straight, fine-pointed for tissue handling, receiving needle, tying knots.
- Smooth-tipped most common, but toothed, curved, angled also available.

## Tools: Forceps - Titanium & Sizes
- Angled forceps useful for reaching under vessels, tying knots, patency tests.
- Modified jeweler's forceps with slender, polished tip to dilate vessels.
- Titanium micro forceps: 0.05 mm (12-0) and 0.1 mm (10-0 to 11-0).
- 0.1 mm is versatile for 9-0 to 11-0.

## Tools: Vascular Clamps - Evolution
- Evolved significantly since bulldog clamps used by Jacobson.
- 1970: Henderson et al. developed clamps requiring small key/screw (unsuitable for <1.5 mm).
- 1974: Acland developed double microvascular clamp with wire frame.
- Largely superseded by Tamai modifications with sliding bar.

## Tools: Vascular Clamps - Design & Pressure
- Ideally atraumatic, sufficient closing pressure to prevent bleeding/slippage.
- Single clamps or double approximator clamps.
- Vein clamps: smaller closing pressure, flat jaw.
- Artery clamps: greater closing pressure, slight incurve at tip.

## Tools: Vascular Clamps - Sizing
- Available in variety of sizes for different vessel diameters.
- Pressure inversely proportional to vessel size.
- Ideal pressure: 5–10 g/mm² (largest vessels) and 15–20 g/mm² (smallest vessels).
- Use smallest appropriate clamp to minimize crushing.

## Tools: Vascular Clamps - Limitations
- Can cause intimal lesions.
- Occupy space in confined sites.
- Risk of backwalling due to vessel flattening.
- Plaque-filled atherosclerotic vessels pose a challenge.

## Tools: Clampless Anastomosis
- Thermosensitive gel clinically proven in cardiovascular surgery.
- Provides circular stenting and gentle distension for blood-free site.
- Dissolves completely with cold saline irrigation after anastomosis.
- May find way in atherosclerotic arteries and confined sites.

## Tools: Bipolar Coagulator
- Developed in 1956, promoted microsurgery by attaining bloodless field.
- Conducts current between tips of jeweler’s forceps.
- Heat damage only within very small area between tips.
- Precise coagulation of small branches as close as 2 mm to main vessel.
- Power setting must be optimized to avoid spreading heat.

## Tools: Irrigation - Purposes & Methods
- Clear view of vessel walls is imperative.
- Constant irrigation with Ringer’s lactate or heparinized saline.
- Purposes:
  - Prevent desiccation of vessels
  - Prevent sticking of suture to tissue
  - Wash away blood and clots
  - Wash away prothrombotic factors
- Performed through continuous system or syringe with lacrimal cannula.

## Tools: Suction
- Small amount of blood may obscure field.
- Methods vary:
  - Suction through moistened hydrocellulose sponge/gauze
  - Suction tubes draining through perforated background plate
  - Homemade suction tips with intravascular catheter
- Cellulose spearheads (eye sponges) afford precise control for small ooze.

## Tools: Microsutures - History & Materials
- Buncke made first microneedle by drilling hole in 75 mm stainless steel wire.
- Held single strand of silk for rabbit ear replantation.
- Acland developed commercially available needle.
- Commonest suture: non-resorbable nylon (low tissue reactivity, good knot-holding).
- Polypropylene preferred by some (slides and handles better).

## Tools: Microsutures - Sizes & Needles
- Sizes: 8-0 to 12-0.
- 9-0: Vessels ≥2 mm (100 µm curved needle).
- 10-0: Vessels 1–2 mm (70–100 µm curved needle).
- 11-0 to 12-0: Smaller vessels (50–75 µm or 50 µm curved needle).
- Needle length: 5.1 mm preferred for 9-0/10-0; 3.6 mm for 11-0/12-0.
- Shapes: three-eighths circle, half-circle, or straight. Tips: round, tapered, spatula.

## Tools: Anastomotic Devices - UNILINK
- Microsutures do not fully meet criteria of "ideal" anastomosis.
- 1962: Nakayama introduced metallic rings and interlocking pins.
- 1986: Östrup and Berggren developed UNILINK system.
- Currently marketed as Microvascular Anastomotic COUPLER System.
- Two disposable high-density polyethylene rings with 6-8 stainless-steel pins.

## Tools: Anastomotic Devices - Features & Patency
- Simple, fast, does not disturb intima.
- Excellent patency rates up to 100%, even in irradiated fields.
- Rings sized 1 to 4 mm (vessels 0.8–4.3 mm, max wall thickness 0.5 mm).
- Suitable for end-to-end and end-to-side anastomosis.

## Tools: Anastomotic Devices - Contraindications
- Peripheral vascular disease.
- Areas with ongoing radiation therapy.
- Active infection.
- Concurrent diabetes and corticosteroid therapy.
- Arterial contraindications: thick-walled vessels, diameter discrepancy >1.5:1, non-pliable vessels, artery <1.5 mm.

## Tools: Absorbable Couplers & Staplers
- Absorbable anastomotic coupler developed to resolve permanent rigid ring.
- Patency rates 92.9–100%; completely absorbed at 70 days to 30 weeks.
- Nonpenetrating microvascular stapler (VCS clip applier system).
- Uses nonpenetrating titanium clips in interrupted, everting fashion.
- Reduced anastomotic time and higher patency rate.

## Tools: Other Non-Suture Methods - Glues
- Fibrin glues and cyanoacrylate glues studied.
- Fibrin glue: imitates final pathway in coagulation.
- Reduces number of sutures and anastomotic time.
- Concerns: glue entering lumen, allergic reactions, anaphylaxis.
- Cyanoacrylates: plagued by histotoxicity, foreign-body granulomatous response, thinning of vessel wall.

## Tools: Other Non-Suture Methods - Welding
- Thermal or laser energy welding.
- Laser types: Nd:YAG, CO2, argon, diode lasers.
- Up to 100% patency rates, better blood flow in veins.
- Laser-activated protein solders introduced for strength.
- Fear of weakening and pseudoaneurysm formation limits clinical use.

## General Principles: Success Factors
- Success is multifactorial.
- Technical skills in vessel anastomosis are a must-have craft.
- Learning 100%-patent microanastomoses is the first step to becoming competent.

## General Principles: The Working Environment
- Prerequisites: calm disposition and patience.
- Concentrate without unnecessary interruptions; do not hurry.
- Inadvisable to work too long at a stretch; take breaks.
- Competent assistant and specialized scrub nurse make a big difference.
- Endurance and perseverance are virtues.

## General Principles: Training
- "Some are born microsurgeons while others become so through discipline and training."
- Traditional apprenticeship model not readily applied.
- Special microsurgery apprenticeship in form of fellowship is a must.
- Can start in laboratory (gloves, silicone tubes, rat models).

## General Principles: Training in Clinical Setting
- Trainees can learn from senior surgeons in clinical setting without lab courses.
- Given opportunity to do second vein first.
- After steady patency, arterial anastomosis handed to them under supervision.
- Must do both vein and artery well under supervision multiple times before independence.

## General Principles: Training - Support & Honesty
- Trainees not left completely alone; given reasonable time.
- Encouraged to report honestly without fear.
- Call for help instead of wasting precious time.
- If deviation from acceptable standards, experienced member takes over immediately.

## General Principles: Planning and Positioning
- Time spent planning and positioning is never wasted.
- Right position makes movements easier and procedure faster.
- Comfort relates directly to success.
- Poor planning results in fatigue, frustration, and failure.

## General Principles: Surgeon Posture & Microscope
- Choose right incisions and patient positioning (two-team approach reduces time).
- Surgeon positioned comfortably, preferably on self-adjustable stool.
- Legs under table, feet flat on ground for stable base.
- Forearms rest on folded drapes at level of anastomosis to minimize tremor.
- Microscope positioned to not obstruct movement but provide maximum control.

## General Principles: Securing the Flap or Flap Inset
- Inset considered before anastomosis is performed.
- After circulation restored, flap swells and bleeds, making inset difficult.
- Inset performed first ensures good hemostasis before pedicle divided.
- Allows accurate judgment of pedicle length, avoiding tension or redundancy.

## General Principles: Flap Thinning & Tailoring
- Tailoring or thinning flap better performed while perfused.
- Either before pedicle division or after microanastomoses.
- Allows better control of bleeders and avoids hematoma.
- Exception: Breast surgery where anastomosis lies deep to inset.

## General Principles: Selection of Recipient Vessels
- Use healthy recipient vessels of appropriate size with good flow.
- Ideally away from zones of trauma, irradiation, inflammation, fibrosis, scarring.
- Healthy vessel: soft wall, vascular sheath easily dissected.
- Traumatized vessels encased in fibrotic tissue, prone to bleeding.

## General Principles: Vascular Assessment
- Assess presence and quality of recipient vessels (especially post-irradiation, trauma, DVT, diabetes).
- Recipient vessels do not have to be classic big vessels; perforating branches can be used.
- Veins also considered, far more important in lymphatic reconstruction.
- Assessment via Doppler ultrasound, Angiography/CTA, ICG imaging, lymphoscintigraphy.

## General Principles: Recipient Vessel Preparation
- Dissection under loupes or microscope magnification.
- Free sufficient length for tension-free anastomosis.
- Depends on flap pedicle length, depth of recipient vessels, size, technique.
- Deep vessels (e.g., internal thoracic) require greater length to orient superficially.

## General Principles: Artery Assessment
- Gross trimming of adventitia performed around anastomosis area.
- Check quality of artery and vein under microscope.
- Inspect for signs of damage indicating need for more proximal dissection.
- Expansile pulsation indicates adequacy, confirmed by healthy spurting.
- If no spurt, check normotension, relieve vasospasm, or cut back.

## General Principles: Vein Assessment
- Ideal recipient vein at least as wide as flap vein.
- Smaller vein may produce bottle-neck effect.
- Divided to assess quality; good outflow indicates healthy vessel.
- If doubt, flush with heparinized saline via small catheter.
- Little resistance means likely to drain well; high pressure means tie off tributaries.

## General Principles: Vessel Setup
- Irrigate during and after dissection with heparinized saline.
- Cover with 2–4% lidocaine or 3% papaverine-soaked gauze to prevent desiccation/vasospasm.
- Place vessel ends in double approximating clamp under magnification.
- Choose appropriate clamp size for adequate length between clamps.

## General Principles: Background & Hemostasis
- Moist gauze beneath vessel setup elevates plane and orients vessels horizontally.
- Serves as wick to mop up pooling fluids.
- Silastic tube attached to suction facilitates drainage without sucking vessels.
- Pliable nonadherent, nonreflective background material placed under vessels.
- Good hemostasis maintained at all times; trickle of blood obstructs field and causes thrombus.

## General Principles: Preparation of Vessels - Luminal Inspection
- Inspect lumens for irregularities (Figure 25.2):
  - Intimal tears or separation from media
  - Thrombi
  - Atherosclerotic plaques
  - Friable calcified walls
- Gently irrigate debris away (Figure 25.3) or atraumatically remove with microforceps.
- If failing, cut back to healthier vessel segment, possibly using interpositional vein graft.

## General Principles: Vessel Wall Layers (Figure 25.4)
- Tunica intima: single layer of endothelium on basal lamina.
- Subendothelial layer adjacent to internal elastic lamina.
- Tunica media: mainly smooth-muscle cells, thickest layer of arterial wall.
- Tunica adventitia: outermost layer, loose areolar connective tissue containing vasa vasorum.
- Veins have same layers but less defined, tunica media much thinner.

## General Principles: Adventitia Trimming (Figures 25.5 & 25.6)
- Loose adventitia peeled off or sharply trimmed parallel to luminal edge.
- Distance of 3–4 mm from anastomotic site.
- Sharp dissection causes less damage to vessel.
- Purpose: improve visualization, prevent adventitia falling into lumen.
- Avoid overly aggressive stripping to prevent necrosis and false aneurysms.

## General Principles: Vessel Dilation & Approximation (Figures 25.7 & 25.8)
- Lumens gently dilated in two planes with vessel dilator or microneedle holder.
- Stretch maintained for one second.
- Aids suturing, prevents vasospasm, flushes out blood, overcomes size discrepancy.
- Hemostat artery forceps brings clamps together so ends touch or minimally overlap.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Artery vs. Vein
- No consensus on optimal sequence.
- Dictated by ischemia time and relative vessel position.
- Deeper, more difficult vessel repaired first.
- Arterial repair first shortens warm ischemia time.
- Re-establishment of circulation reveals dominant venous drainage and detects pedicle twist/kink.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Venous Congestion
- Disadvantage of artery first: flap may start bleeding, affecting vein anastomosis.
- Venous congestion may increase bleeding and free radicals.
- Avoid by intermittently releasing second vein or allowing less dominant vein to drain freely.
- Venous anastomosis first allows better adjustment of pedicle length but delays revascularization.

## Anastomoses Sequence: Single vs. Dual Venous
- Some advocate two venous anastomoses to avoid venous insufficiency.
- Khouri et al. reported higher failure rate with only one venous anastomosis (4.3% vs. 0%).
- Single venous anastomosis to suitable recipient vein provides adequate drainage and reduces operative time.
- Sound judgment required; if first vein unreliable, perform second.

## Suturing Techniques: End-to-End Overview
- Most common method used.
- Simple and appropriate for most arterial and venous anastomoses.
- Halving, triangulation, or “back wall-up” technique can be used.
- Carrel's principles: avoid luminal narrowing, avoid folds, oppose intimal edges closely.

## Suturing Techniques: Triangulation & Stay Sutures (Figure 25.9)
- Carrel: three stay sutures at 120° from each other.
- Cobbett modified: two stay sutures at 120°.
- Tensioning apart makes longer back wall fall away, reducing chance of through-stitch.
- Alternative: two stay sutures at 180° angle to ensure even spacing.

## Suturing Techniques: Needle Penetration & Knot Tying (Figure 25.10)
- Second stay suture is most important and difficult.
- Needle penetrates vessel wall perpendicularly, incorporating all layers (especially intima).
- Size of bite determined by wall thickness and suture, maintained throughout.
- First throw double to maintain tension, followed by two single throws.
- Knots snugged by sight, not feel, until edges meet and slightly evert.

## Suturing Techniques: Tension & Through-Stitching
- Sutures too tight: small tears expose subendothelium, allow platelet aggregation and thrombus.
- Can damage media; if 1/3 of wall undergoes necrosis, re-endothelialization fails, occlusion follows.
- Tight sutures may narrow anastomosis site.
- Sutures placed between stay sutures, aiming for smallest number to achieve leakproof anastomosis.

## Suturing Techniques: Back Wall Suturing (Figures 25.11 & 25.12)
- Approximator clamp turned over.
- Back wall sutured by placing suture midway between stay sutures.
- Leave last few stitches untied until last suture placed to maintain visualization.
- Leave apparent gaps alone until clamp released to prevent through stitching.
- Back wall-up technique employed if clamp cannot be turned over.

## Suturing Techniques: Continuous Suturing (Figure 25.13)
- Suitable for minimally size-discrepant vessels >2 or 3 mm.
- Reduces anastomosis time by nearly half, more hemostatic.
- Problems: suture entanglement, risk of purse-string constriction.
- Place two or three stay sutures, leave one end long.
- Running sutures placed at regular intervals, tied to next stay suture.

## Suturing Techniques: Open-Loop Suturing (Figure 25.14)
- Combines convenience of continuous with advantages of interrupted.
- Running suture performed leaving small loops, or between two stay stitches.
- First suture tied, ends cut short.
- Next loop pulled through, tied, and cut.
- Reduces maneuvers, maintains lumen visualization, eliminates purse-stringing risk.

## Suturing Techniques: Sleeve Anastomosis (Figure 25.15)
- Introduced by Lauritzen in 1978 ("end-in-end").
- Telescopes vessels using two extraluminal sutures pulling one vessel inside the other.
- Fewer sutures, reduced time and trauma.
- Low patency rates reported by some prevented popularity.
- Modification by Riggio et al. ("hemi-invagination") improved patency to 95–100% in rats.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Indications
- Useful for significant vessel size or wall thickness discrepancy.
- Need to preserve distal circulation (e.g., single-vessel leg).
- Anecdotally less prone to vessel spasm in lower extremity.
- Higher success rates, but not necessarily higher patency rates than end-to-end.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Arteriotomy (Figure 25.16)
- Arteriotomy or venotomy made in recipient vessel.
- Triangular, elliptical, or simple longitudinal slit.
- Hole should not have irregular edges.
- Sufficient length dissected for two clamps; adventitia trimmed circumferentially.
- Baby Satinsky clamp useful to maintain flow and less traumatic.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Suturing Techniques (Figure 25.17)
- Single stitch taken transversely as stay suture.
- Vessel around suture excised using microvascular scissors and extended with No. 11 blade.
- Acland–Banis arteriotomy clamp can also be used to excise ellipse.
- Opening should not be longer than diameter of donor vessel.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Godina's Technique
- If flap vessel long enough, stay stitches at distal and proximal ends.
- "Front" wall completed before pulling vessel to perform "back" wall.
- If insufficient length, wall further from you must be performed first.
- Sutures placed radially to center of arteriotomy.
- Persistent leakage if sutures placed transversely.

## End-to-Side Anastomosis: Advantages & Studies
- Godina: higher success rate, greater freedom of operative planning, technical simplicity.
- Study of >2000 anastomoses: end-to-end and end-to-side equally effective when properly applied.
- Patency approached 100%.
- End-to-side venous anastomosis had higher success rate in rat study.
- Slit technique easier to perform in vessels <1.5 mm.

## Use of the Coupler: Sizing & Loading
- Most common alternative to conventional suture.
- Time-saving, equivalent patency rates.
- Outer diameter of each vessel measured after gentle dilatation.
- In size-discrepant vessels, coupler chosen matching internal diameter to smaller vessel's outer diameter.
- Coupler loaded on anastomotic instrument, ensuring it is well seated.

## Use of the Coupler: Impalement & Assembly (Figure 25.18)
- Instrument placed perpendicular to vessels, vessel end threaded through ring.
- Edges impaled securely on first pin (bite 1–2 pin diameters with adequate intimal bite).
- Impale on every other pin first to ensure even spacing.
- Draping flap vessel first allows easier position.
- Rings brought together by turning handle clockwise, reinforced with hemostat.
- Ejected by turning handle counterclockwise.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Size-Discrepant Vessels
- Commonly encountered despite careful planning.
- More problems if inflow big/flap artery small, or outflow big/recipient vein small.
- Sudden change of caliber causes turbulence predisposing to thrombosis.
- Mismatches up to 4:1 can be anastomosed end-to-end depending on skills.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Managing Size Discrepancy (Figure 25.19)
- Simplest method: gently stretch smaller vessel mechanically.
- Place interrupted sutures further apart on larger vessel.
- Fish-mouth incision or oblique cut on smaller vessel reduces discrepancy.
- Angles >30° of oblique cut may cause kinking, avoid.
- Anastomosis just distal to side branch opening up distal wall.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Large Discrepancies & Wall Thickness
- Discrepancy >3:1: consider end-to-side, vein graft, or side branch of larger vessel.
- Last resort: smaller vessel dilated maximally, sutured widely to larger vessel.
- Remaining vessel sutured to itself; obliquely placed surgical clip tapers vessel to minimize turbulence.
- Wall thickness discrepancy: gentle dilatation thins wall.
- Key: take equal bites of intima from both vessels.

## Difficult Anastomosis: Vertically Oriented Anastomosis
- Most challenging configuration of vessels.
- If possible, change position of body part, adjust position or table.
- Free up more vessel length to manipulate into horizontal plane using gauze.
- If position cannot be changed and limited space: reduce magnification.
- Reducing magnification increases depth of field, reducing need to alter focus constantly.

## Atherosclerosis and Loose Intima: Challenges
- Commonly encountered due to elderly patients and cardiovascular disease.
- Radiotherapy also causes irradiation-induced atherosclerosis.
- Significant plaque: cut back to healthier intima or choose another vessel.
- Artery divided with sharp scissors in one cut to minimize separation of atherosclerotic intima.

## Atherosclerosis: Trimming & Clamping Precautions
- Plaques can create false lumen or intraluminal flap causing thrombosis.
- Cut edge trimmed slowly and circumferentially (like opening a can).
- Vascular clamp should not exert too much tension (fractures calcified walls).
- Provide proper micro-clamp tension only in areas not affected by atherosclerosis.
- Consider venous microclamps for both artery and vein to apply less pressure.

## Atherosclerosis: Suturing Techniques (Figure 25.20)
- Round needle useful; meticulous placement of interrupted sutures using smallest microsuture.
- Intima visualized at all times.
- Suture ideally passed from inside lumen of atherosclerotic vessel to outside.
- Avoids further separation of intima from vessel wall.
- Double-needle suture useful if both recipient and donor diseased.

## Atherosclerosis: End-to-Side Risks
- Vessel dilatation should be avoided.
- Careful vessel wall eversion avoids leaving raw areas exposed to blood flow.
- Too much tension may erode plaque and tear vessel wall.
- End-to-end preferred over end-to-side.
- End-to-side causes more direct exposure of plaque and edges, increasing thrombus risk.
- If end-to-side unavoidable, use end-to-end after providing T or Y vein graft.

## Microvascular Grafts: Indications & Harvest
- Increased storehouse of flaps diminished need for vein grafts.
- Still necessary in trauma, vessel-depleted neck, re-explorations.
- Indications: recipient vessel out of reach, under tension, considerable size mismatch, outside zone of injury/radiation.
- Harvest done with loupe magnification.
- Ideally match caliber of vessels to be anastomosed.

## Microvascular Grafts: Donor Veins & Handling
- Upper limb defects bridged with upper limb veins.
- Work-horse: great/lesser saphenous vein (length, two-team approach).
- Alternatives: cephalic, comitant veins of free flap.
- Volar forearm and dorsal foot veins preferred in finger/hand replantation.
- Vein handled minimally, tributaries ligated/coagulated.
- All vein grafts need dilatation prior to anastomosis for wall-thickness match.

## Microvascular Grafts: Direction & Hydrodilatation
- Length marked out; remember vein grafts contract after division, lengthen after high-pressure flow.
- Direction crucial: must always have antegrade flow.
- Proximal end marked with surgical clip.
- Hydrodilatation stretches graft, untwists vein, relieves vasospasm, visualizes bleeding points.
- Open end anastomosed first, clamp released to check direction and length.

## Microvascular Grafts: Arterial Grafts
- Advantages over vein grafts:
  - Absence of valves
  - Anatomical taper
  - Similar luminal and wall-thickness profiles
  - Better handling characteristics
- Maintain endothelium, less subintimal hyperplasia.
- Produce more prostacyclin relative to vein grafts in first 3 weeks.
- Not shown to have significant advantages in context of microvascular surgery.

## Testing Patency: Observation & Characteristics
- Assessed after completion of each anastomosis.
- Arterial pulsation: expansile or longitudinal.
- Longitudinal (in long axis) is sign of partial/complete thrombosis.
- Flap shows no return of circulation; anastomosis should be redone.
- Good flow from vein indicates patency.
- Recipient vein fills well, natural round diameter = patent.
- Engorged, dark blood column = thrombosed.

## Testing Patency: Simple Tests (Figure 25.21)
- "Uplift" test: gently hook up thin-walled vessel until column almost occluded.
- Patent: alternate filling and collapsing with each pulse.
- Empty-and-refill test: slightly more traumatic, preferably on veins.
- Gently occlude vessel distal to anastomosis.
- Empty segment with second forceps by running in direction of flow.
- Release first forceps; emptied segment should refill immediately.
- Sluggish or absent refill = not patent.

## Testing Patency: Modern Adjuncts
- Use of side branches provides atraumatic way to assess flow.
- Requires awareness during dissection to keep side branches.
- ICG (Indocyanine green) imaging: easier and more accurate.
- Many microscopes equipped with infrared cameras.
- Hand-held devices available to examine flap perfusion.
